articleTitle: South Africa revealed through her wonder sights and cities. Tavern of the southern seas
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: There are few more arresting spectacles in the Southern Hemisphere than that provided by Table Mountain at Capetown. As far back as 1580 the remark, “Fairest Cape in all the world.” was made by Eng. land's famous Admiral, Drake, who anchored in the shade of Table Mountain in the course of his trail-blazing voyage round the globe, and it is not so very long since a newspaper in Capetown quoted the words: “Your skyline beats them all,” uttered by a woman member of an American world-cruise party. It. is a far cry from the Elizabethan diction of Drake to the terse English of the twentieth century woman, but the lapse of time discloses no difference in the purport of the respective utterances. And in the interim countless testimonies have been given on the subject of Table Mountain. With every traveller whose eyes have beheld it, the effect has been one of instant appeal, for there is an air of distinction about this grey-faced mountain which impresses not alone by reason of its bulk and height, but by its poise and dignity as well. For all the nobility of aspect, however, Nature has not been above striking a likeness, in the essential outlines of this mountain, to one of the commonplaces of life. There is no mistaking the suggestion conveyed by its formation, rectangular and flat-lopped as it is, and the similitude is even less liable to misinterpretation if the mountain is encountered at dawn, when the clouds that invariably hang on the summit look for all the world like a laundered table-cloth.

abstract: Mr. President and gentlemen, this paper is, I think, of special value because it presents comparative data for operating experience with and without the use of Petersen Coils under conditions which are exceptionally unfavourable to the coils. The conditions on the 40 kV system are probably as unfavourable as could be found anywhere, firstly because the system is an old one involving many weak places, and secondly because the system is situated on a plateau prone to very severe and frequent lightning storms where, owing to the rocky nature of the ground, low footing resistances cannot be obtained. If Petersen coils can make a satisfactory showing under these conditions there should be no question of their value under move average conditions.

abstract: The contribution of Messrs, Allan and Bozzoli has no doubt been of greatest interest to the electrical engineer. It was unfortunate that my work followed instead of preceding theirs, as I am sure that all who saw specimens of burnt wonderstone at the Empire Exhibition were impressed by the fine finish. However, I agree with Mr. Gillette that wonderstone will never replace porcelain as a high grade insulator. The value of wonderstone is as an insulator at high temperatures. For example, Mr. D. A. P. Wilson (private communication) found that porcelain was quite unsatisfactory in an electric sintering press. Wonderstone, on the other hand, proved very successful, and is being used continuously in experimental work in the production of electrically sintered diamond drill crowns (1). In another case a wonderstone former was found to be superior to various types of fibre board formers, to support the asbestos insulated wire of an induction heater, operating continuously at 150°C.
